title: Rule Card (array file) — one business rule of the reference, cited
description: Lane R of G1, written to findings/rules/<domain>.yaml. Lane D mines entities, routes, permissions, jobs and events; the rules that make those routes DO something — the interest calculation, the eligibility check, the state machine on a work package — were not a lane-D target, so they surfaced for the first time at G5 when spec-writer had to re-read the source to write acceptance criteria. That re-read is the drift point: two agents, weeks apart, deriving the same rule from the same file and not necessarily agreeing. A Rule Card moves the derivation to G1, where it is evidenced, judged and locked with the taxonomy. Gate 1 locks this directory alongside matrix/features.yaml — rules are taxonomy, not design.

allOf.description: `when` is required for every kind but `invariant`, and `entities` is required for `invariant` alone. An invariant has no trigger — its writers are every operation that writes its entities — so a forced `when` would be a second list of those writers, drifting from the first.
`transition` belongs to `state-transition` cards only. On any other kind it would feed validate.py's state-machine assembly with an edge the card does not claim.

id.description: R-<DOMAIN>-<NNN>. Same pattern family as F-<DOMAIN>-<NNN> on purpose: a spec's acceptance criterion cites both, and two id shapes that differ only in prefix are two things a reader can hold at once.

kind.description: Fixed enum. `calculation` produces a number, `validation` accepts or rejects an input, `eligibility` decides whether an actor may do a thing, `state-transition` moves an entity between states, `derivation` computes a field from others. Those five fire on a trigger, and one that seems to need a sixth trigger-kind is usually two rules. `invariant` is the one kind with no trigger: a property that holds after EVERY write to its entities ("an invoice's total equals the sum of its line items plus tax"). Before it existed, a miner split such a property into one card per operation that happened to preserve it; each card passed, the property itself was written down nowhere, and a rebuild could add a writer that broke it with no card to fail. A constraint the reference's database enforces (CHECK, unique index, foreign key, NOT NULL) is lane D's, transcribed into the schema findings and the ERD, and is not a card.

path_kind.description: Which side of the behavior the rule is on. `error`: what happens when an operation fails — a rescue, a rollback, a compensation, a retry, the error response. `default`: what happens when an input is missing — the fallback value, the implied setting. A field rather than a kind because it is a different axis: a state transition can be on the error path, and so can a validation. These are the rules a rebuild drops silently — a rescue that swallows an exception has no test, so nothing fails when it is gone — and before this field nothing asked a miner for them or counted how many were found. Named `path_kind`, not `path`, because an evidence entry's `path` already means a file.

transition.description: The edge a `state-transition` card describes, in a form a script can assemble. Each card is one edge, in prose, so an entity's state machine was N unrelated cards and a state no transition reached was invisible; validate.py now builds the machine per entity and field from these, and reports unreachable states, dead ends and a missing creation transition. Optional, not required: requiring it would fail every state-transition card mined before it existed, and past Gate 1 those cards sit under a locked path — adding a field nobody asked for at the time would take a gate reopen.

entity.description: Must also appear in the card's `entities[]` — validate.py fails the card otherwise, since two fields on one card disagreeing is a defect, not a coverage question.

field.description: The attribute holding the state (`status`). One entity can carry two machines, `status` and `pdf_status`; they are assembled separately.

from.description: Every state this edge leaves from. `(none)` for creation — the state a new record starts in.

to.description: The state the edge arrives in.

given.description: The precondition. Executable-style Gherkin, concrete values over prose. For an `invariant`, the scope the property holds over ("for every INVOICE in status issued or later").

when.description: The trigger. One behavior per card — an `and` in here usually means two cards. Omitted for an `invariant`.

then.description: The observable outcome, with the concrete values a test could assert on. This is the sentence the judge re-derives against the cited line, so it has to be checkable against source rather than a paraphrase of intent. For an `invariant`, the property itself, with values.

evidence.description: Same shape as finding.schema.json's evidence, with `basis` required rather than optional — a rule with no stated provenance is the thing this lane exists to stop. `line` is what makes a card re-derivable: the judge opens path at commit and reads that line.

then.description: `transcribed` asserts the rule was copied out of the reference's source at the pinned commit. Without a line there is nothing to re-derive against — the judge would be re-reading a whole file to confirm a sentence, which is the work the citation exists to save.

features.description: Which matrix entries this rule belongs to. validate.py resolves every id against matrix/features.yaml — a card citing a feature that does not exist is a card no spec will ever find.

entities.description: Entities the rule reads or writes. validate.py checks each against findings/ground-truth/reference-erd*.mermaid: a rule naming an entity the reference does not have is a rule that was inferred rather than mined. Required for an `invariant`: these are the entities the property is OF, and G5 finds every module that must test it by the entities that module writes.

verification.description: Set by rubric-judge, never by the miner: `re-derived` means the judge opened the cited path at the commit and line and confirmed `then` is supported there. A card asserting its own verification would be the miner grading its own homework, which is the whole reason this field is written by a different agent.

notes.description: Anything a reader needs that is not the rule itself — a reference quirk, a case deliberately excluded, an upstream issue number.
